source.title: Learning to Reweight Examples for Robust Deep Learning
source.authors: Mengye Ren; Wenyuan Zeng; Binh Yang; R. Urtasun

record.tranche_reason: Reports CIFAR test accuracy as label-noise levels vary, but uses a learned example-reweighting method and does not reproduce the original random-label fitting setup.
record.gate_note: The Introduction cites Zhang et al. (2017) for fitting arbitrary label-flip noise; that cited result is not this study's result. The study's own noise-sweep outcomes bear on V4, but do not establish perfect training fit or test error at chance.
record.test_reason: The standard ResNet-32 baseline supplies an own-study result on V4's generalization component in a new, background-flip noise setting: test accuracy drops by more than 40 percentage points as corruption increases from 0% to 50%. The reweighting method's comparative performance alone does not test the memorization claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that their online validation-guided reweighting algorithm improves robustness to class imbalance, noisy labels, and their combination, and is expected to train end-to-end without additional hyperparameter search.
record.recipe_differences: Uses online meta-learning to reweight examples based on a clean validation set; the tested noise experiments are not the original random-label memorization setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise level and noise type (uniform flip versus background flip); clean validation-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed reweighting method loses only six percentage points of test accuracy over the 0–50% noise sweep and improves noisy-label benchmark performance using clean validation data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Validation-guided example reweighting improves robustness to label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: After the first learning-rate decay, baseline and S-Model validation performance deteriorates, which the authors attribute to overfitting training noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Continued training can worsen generalization under background-flip label noise.

record.problems: The random-label memorization result is cited from prior work, not measured here. The noise-sweep training curves are figure-only in the supplied text, and the reported text does not quantify training error across noise levels or establish test error at chance.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the text's noise-sweep figures include training curves, but the supplied text gives no separately assignable numerical training-error results, and the prose does not state that training fit is perfect at each noise level. Table 1 and Table 2 compare noisy-label methods at 40% noise, but do not test the versions' random-label or smooth-degradation claims.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown with increasing corruption. The reported approximately threefold overhead concerns the reweighting algorithm instead.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across corruption levels; the full sweep to completely random labels and chance test performance; and whether degradation is steady throughout that sweep. The supplied prose establishes an endpoint decline over 0–50% background-flip noise.
Whether the named regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them impairs true-label generalization.

Separate learning trajectories for real-label patterns and noisy labels establishing their learning order. Aggregate validation deterioration attributed to noise overfitting does not directly establish that ordering.

missing.what: The prose explicitly quantifies the baseline's test-accuracy decline as more than 40 percentage points between 0% and 50% noise. Although rows_left_out declares the figure sweep omitted, its rationale overlooks this extractable textual result. Add a baseline endpoint-comparison row linked to V4.
missing.locator: Section 4.3, Impact of the noise level; Figure 5.

record.verdict_notes: The arbitrary-noise fitting statement in the introduction is attributed to Zhang et al. and is not this study's result. No numerical training-accuracy values can be recovered reliably from the supplied figure text. The V4 verdict concerns only the measured generalization component; missing measurements do not justify a limits_scope or challenges verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison for fitting random versus true labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The study reports a noise-level test-accuracy trend, but does not report numerical training error showing perfect fit at each noise level, nor establish that test error reaches chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation permit random-label fitting, or whether removing them affects true-label generalization.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, or whether these are learned differently over training.

relationships.condition: Standard ResNet-32 baseline on CIFAR background-flip noise, comparing 0% with 50% corruption; generalization component only.
relationships.reason: Based on Section 4.3 text accompanying Figure 5, rather than extracted rows: baseline test accuracy drops by more than 40 percentage points as noise increases. This supports degradation with corruption, without establishing perfect training fit or the full trajectory.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy dropped by more than 40 percentage points between clean labels and 50% corruption.
